banks: The instruction for {subject} in {place} should name the tenant who is home after work, because the side gate stays locked until someone is in, so the visit is diary-dated only once that person has agreed the hour.

The instruction for {subject} in {place} should name a managing agent who holds the spare set, because the keys have to be collected from a named office before the van leaves Stockport, so the quote records the keyholder rather than assuming the house is empty.

The instruction for {subject} in {place} should name the landlord who will meet the engineer at the front door, because parking is on the street and the bell is the top flat, so the written quote names that meeting point before anyone travels.

The instruction for {subject} in {place} should name a neighbour who has been asked to open up, because the household is away and the neighbour is only free before noon, so the instruction says so, instead of leaving an engineer waiting on the step.

The instruction for {subject} in {place} should name the caretaker of a small block, because the stair is in use and the plant cupboard is locked, so access to the cupboard is agreed before the day, not discovered on the landing.

The instruction for {subject} in {place} should name an inventory clerk who is already booked at the void, because the check-out and the repair visit can clash if nobody compares the times, so the office asks which appointment is first.

The instruction for {subject} in {place} should name the householder who works nights, because a morning slot would arrive while they are asleep, so the booking is offered for the afternoon they have named.

The instruction for {subject} in {place} should name a relative who is looking after the property, because they do not live there and need a day's notice, so the quote is sent to the person who can actually approve it.

The instruction for {subject} in {place} should name the letting negotiator for that branch, because they want the report uploaded to the agency portal the same day, so the instruction names the portal and the file name they expect.

The instruction for {subject} in {place} should name the tenant of a room in a shared house, because other residents must not be walked through without warning, so the note lists which rooms are in the scope and which stay shut.

The instruction for {subject} in {place} should name the block manager, because the entrance door releases on a fob the engineer will not have, so someone from the building is booked to meet them at the street door.

The instruction for {subject} in {place} should name the owner of a holiday let between stays, because the cleaners are in during the changeover, so the visit is placed either before the clean or after it, not in the middle.

The instruction for {subject} in {place} should name a warden at a sheltered scheme, because residents worry if an unknown van is on the drive, so the warden is told the registration and the rough arrival.

The instruction for {subject} in {place} should name the tenant who has a dog, because the dog needs to be in another room while work is in the kitchen or the hall, so that arrangement is written on the booking, not improvised at the door.

The instruction for {subject} in {place} should name the agent covering a vacant flat above a shop, because the shop stairs are the only way up and the shop opens at nine, so the visit is agreed with the shop so the stair is free.

The instruction for {subject} in {place} should name the landlord's builder who is already on site, because two trades in one room will get in each other's way, so the quote says whether we attend with them or after they have finished.

The instruction for {subject} in {place} should name a housing officer, because the property is a temporary let and the occupant changes often, so the instruction names who is actually living there this week.

The instruction for {subject} in {place} should name the tenant who will be at work, because a key safe code is the only way in, so the code is taken by phone on the day and is not left in an email thread.

The instruction for {subject} in {place} should name the freeholder's agent, because the demise and the common parts are different jobs, so the quote says which of the two we have been asked to attend.

The instruction for {subject} in {place} should name the person who paid the deposit, because they want to be present when anything in the check-in report is discussed, so the appointment is offered at a time they can attend.

The instruction for {subject} in {place} should name a local caretaker who covers several streets, because they cannot be at two houses at once, so the running order of the addresses is agreed the day before.

The instruction for {subject} in {place} should name the occupant of an annexe, because the annexe has its own door and its own meter, so the booking says which door and which supply the job is about.

Keys for {subject} in {place} may involve a coded key safe by the meter box, and the code is confirmed the afternoon before, because codes change, so the engineer does not force a lock because a code has failed.

Keys for {subject} in {place} may involve keys left with a named shop, and the shop closes for lunch and will not hand keys to someone they do not expect, so the shop is told the engineer's name before the morning.
Keys for {subject} in {place} may involve a fob for a communal door and a separate key for the flat, and one without the other wastes the visit, so both are listed on the instruction.

Keys for {subject} in {place} may involve an alarm that is set while the house is empty, and the code has to be given to the person attending, not written on the job sheet in the van, so the panel is left set only if the instruction says to set it.
Keys for {subject} in {place} may involve a gate padlock as well as the front door, and the side access is the one the materials have to use, so both locks are mentioned, not just the front door.

Keys for {subject} in {place} may involve a key for the boiler cupboard that the tenant does not hold, and the cupboard key is with the agent, so the agent is asked for it before the day so the appliance can actually be seen.

Keys for {subject} in {place} may involve a concierge desk that holds fobs for contractors, and the desk wants identification and a job reference, so the reference on the quote is the one the concierge has been given.

Keys for {subject} in {place} may involve a roller shutter on a commercial unit, and the shutter is on a separate switch the tenant controls, so someone who can open it is named for the start of the visit.

Keys for {subject} in {place} may involve an internal door that has been locked by a departing tenant, and forcing it is not part of a survey, so the instruction says whether that room is in scope and who unlocks it.

Keys for {subject} in {place} may involve a loft hatch that has been screwed shut, and the survey cannot invent a loft it cannot enter, so the quote says if a screwdriver and a second person are needed for the hatch.

Keys for {subject} in {place} may involve a meter cupboard in the common stair, and the cupboard is often jammed with other residents' belongings, so the caretaker is asked to clear it before the appointment.
Keys for {subject} in {place} may involve a garage that holds the stopcock, and the garage is on a different key to the house, so that key is requested at the same time as the house keys.
Keys for {subject} in {place} may involve a digital lock whose battery is flat, and the backup key is the only way in, so the booking asks where the backup key is before anyone travels.
Keys for {subject} in {place} may involve a fire-door closer that must not be wedged open, and the door is on the escape route, so the visit is planned so the door can shut between trips to the van.

Keys for {subject} in {place} may involve keys that have to be returned the same day, and the agent will not release the next property until the first set is back, so the running order allows the return.
Keys for {subject} in {place} may involve a key safe that is shared with the cleaner, and the cleaner may have the only fob during their slot, so the two appointments are kept apart.
Keys for {subject} in {place} may involve an entry panel that calls a specific flat, and buzzing the wrong flat annoys another resident, so the flat number is on the booking.
Keys for {subject} in {place} may involve a rear alley gate with a council lock, and not every key opens it, so the instruction says whether the alley is needed for access or materials.

Keys for {subject} in {place} may involve a safe in the office where void keys are tagged, and tags go missing when several contractors are in on one morning, so the tag number is written on our note.
Keys for {subject} in {place} may involve a temporary lock fitted after a lockout, and the key the agent holds may no longer match, so the agent confirms the current key before the slot.
Keys for {subject} in {place} may involve a letterbox key for a block, and the engineer does not need the post, but the electrical intake is beside it, so the person who holds that key is named.
Keys for {subject} in {place} may involve a window lock key for a survey of the openings, and the key is in a kitchen drawer the tenant knows and we do not, so the tenant is asked to leave it out.

The written quote for {subject} in {place} names the address and the rooms in scope, rather than a price taken from the number of bedrooms, so that a change of layout is a revised quote, not a surprise on the invoice.

The written quote for {subject} in {place} names who is paying and where the report should be sent, rather than a figure given on the phone before the building is known, so that the written quote is the price that can be accepted.

The written quote for {subject} in {place} names whether the property is occupied, void, or part-way through a check-out, rather than a single rate copied from a different house, so that the scope is rewritten if the condition is not what was described.

The written quote for {subject} in {place} names the certificate or the repair that was actually asked for, rather than a bundle the caller did not request, so that anything extra is offered as its own quote.

The written quote for {subject} in {place} names access limits, such as a room that must stay in use, rather than an assumption that the house will be empty, so that the price allows for the way the household has to live that day.

The written quote for {subject} in {place} names the photographs that were sent and the date they were taken, rather than a guess from a listing photo, so that the survey still looks at the building when the price depends on what is there.

The written quote for {subject} in {place} names the name of the person who is allowed to accept the quote, rather than an open-ended approval from whoever happens to be in, so that work is booked only after that person accepts.

The written quote for {subject} in {place} names a clear line between the survey and any repair that might follow, rather than a repair slipped into a survey price, so that the household can see which visit they have agreed.

The written quote for {subject} in {place} names the parts that are assumed and the parts that are still to be identified, rather than a promise to fit a named part before it has been seen, so that the quote says what happens if the part on site is different.

The written quote for {subject} in {place} names parking, permits, and how far materials have to be carried, rather than a price that pretends the van can stop at the door, so that the carry and the permit are written down when they apply.

The written quote for {subject} in {place} names whether making good is included or left for another trade, rather than a silent assumption that plaster and paint are in, so that the finish line is the one on the quote.

The written quote for {subject} in {place} names the time the household has said the visit may last, rather than an open day that overruns without warning, so that a return visit is booked if the scope cannot finish in that window.

The written quote for {subject} in {place} names which floors or which dwellings in a block are included, rather than a price that quietly covers the whole building, so that dwellings that were not named are not described as done.

The written quote for {subject} in {place} names the documents the agent needs back, and the format they want, rather than a verbal summary with nothing to file, so that the quote lists the certificate or the note that will be sent.

The written quote for {subject} in {place} names a stated exclusion when another trade owns part of the system, rather than a promise to test equipment we have not been asked to touch, so that the boundary is on the page the client accepts.

The written quote for {subject} in {place} names the condition that would make us stop and reprice, rather than a contract that continues at the old figure when the site is different, so that the stop point is written in ordinary language.

The written quote for {subject} in {place} names whether waste leaves the property, rather than rubbish left in the garden described as removed, so that removal is included only when the quote says so.

The written quote for {subject} in {place} names the date the quote stays open, rather than a price treated as valid months later on a changed building, so that a fresh look is offered when the date has passed.

The written quote for {subject} in {place} names the contact who will be on site and the contact who receives the paperwork, rather than one phone number asked to do both jobs when they are different people, so that both names are on the quote when they differ.

The written quote for {subject} in {place} names any published price that truly applies, such as an EICR from £160 or the HMO pack at £561, rather than those figures reused for a different job, so that every other job on the page is price on application.

The written quote for {subject} in {place} names the sequence of addresses when more than one property is booked, rather than a portfolio total that hides which house is which, so that each address has its own line.

The written quote for {subject} in {place} names what the client will have at the end of the visit, rather than a vague promise that everything will be sorted, so that the finished note matches the lines that were accepted.
Where a tenant is in residence during {subject} in {place}, the visit is agreed with them, not only with the agent, and they know which rooms will be entered.
Where children are at home during the day during {subject} in {place}, the work is kept to rooms that can be shut off, and tools are not left where a child can reach them.

Where someone in the house is working from home during {subject} in {place}, power or water is not taken off without a time they have accepted, and the slot avoids their calls when they have told us the hours.
Where a new tenant moves in the next morning during {subject} in {place}, the void work has to finish in time for the check-in, and the quote says whether that turnaround is realistic.

Where the occupier is elderly and needs a little longer at the door during {subject} in {place}, the engineer does not rush the explanation, and the findings are left in writing as well as said aloud.
Where a shift worker sleeps in the daytime during {subject} in {place}, the appointment is moved rather than ringing the bell repeatedly, and the agent is told why the time changed.
Where the household is observing a religious holiday during {subject} in {place}, the visit is not pressed into that day, and another date is offered.
Where there is a baby in the property during {subject} in {place}, noisy work is timed around the sleep they have told us about, and the note on the booking is read before the van is loaded.
Where a carer attends at fixed times during {subject} in {place}, the engineer is not booked across the care visit, and the two schedules are compared before the day is promised.

Where the tenant has asked for a female or male attendance where the job allows a choice during {subject} in {place}, the office says honestly if the diary cannot meet that, and the request is not ignored.

Where students share the house and only one of them will be in during {subject} in {place}, that person is named so the others are not held responsible for access, and the scope is explained to the person who is actually there.

Where the tenant has reported the fault themselves during {subject} in {place}, the agent's version and the tenant's version are both heard, and the quote describes the fault we have been shown, not a guess.

Where someone in the building does not want photographs of their belongings during {subject} in {place}, photos are limited to the failed part and the access, and private rooms outside the scope are not filmed.
Where the occupier speaks little English during {subject} in {place}, the agent arranges a person who can translate the scope, and we do not start on a nod that may not be consent.
Where a notice has already been served during {subject} in {place}, the visit is still agreed with whoever is living there, and we do not treat a notice as permission to walk in.
Where the tenant will be present for the whole visit during {subject} in {place}, they can see what is tested and what is left, and questions are answered in plain language before we leave.
Where only one room is occupied during a refurbishment during {subject} in {place}, that room stays usable, and dust and tools are kept out of it.
Where the household has a hospital appointment the same day during {subject} in {place}, the slot is moved if the times collide, and the quote is not lost because the day changed.
Where a lodger is in a room the landlord forgot to mention during {subject} in {place}, the room is treated as occupied once we know, and the scope is adjusted before work starts.

Where the tenant has children coming home from school at a known time during {subject} in {place}, the noisy part of the job is aimed before that, when the job allows, and the booking records the time they gave us.
Where an occupant is anxious about strangers during {subject} in {place}, the engineer introduces the job and shows the quote, and they are not left wondering who is in the house.

Where the tenancy ends on the day of the visit during {subject} in {place}, we confirm whether we are attending the outgoing or the incoming household, and keys and reports go to the party named on the instruction.
In a shared house booked for {subject} in {place}, a shared kitchen means we ask which appliances are landlord's and which belong to the tenants, and the quote does not mix the two.
In a shared house booked for {subject} in {place}, locks on bedroom doors means we ask a survey of the means of escape has to see those doors, and the person who can open them is booked to be in.

In a shared house booked for {subject} in {place}, a house let by the room means we ask each lock and each detector may be a separate line, and the quote does not pretend the building is a single family home.

In a shared house booked for {subject} in {place}, an attic room created years ago means we ask the escape from that room is part of the conversation when the job is fire or licence related, and we do not ignore a room because it was not on the original plan.

In a shared house booked for {subject} in {place}, a licence condition the council has already written means we ask the quote is matched to that condition when the client sends it, and we do not invent extra duties the licence does not ask for.

In a shared house booked for {subject} in {place}, a basement used as a bedroom means we ask the visit looks at the use the household described, not only the estate-agent label, and the report uses that description.

In a shared house booked for {subject} in {place}, cooking in bedrooms means we ask detectors and doors are discussed against the way the house is actually lived in, and the quote says what we were asked to check.

In a shared house booked for {subject} in {place}, a rear annexe with its own cooking means we ask it may be a separate dwelling for the job in hand, and the instruction says whether the annexe is included.

In a shared house booked for {subject} in {place}, bicycles and bins in the hall means we ask the escape route is photographed only as far as the job requires, and the quote does not become a clear-out unless clearing it was requested.

In a shared house booked for {subject} in {place}, a manager who visits once a week means we ask the day of our visit and their day need to be compared when a door must be opened, and the office asks for that day.
In a shared house booked for {subject} in {place}, notices already on the fire doors means we ask we do not cover them with our own stickers, and defects are written down rather than disguised.

In a shared house booked for {subject} in {place}, a mixed house of workers on different shifts means we ask there is rarely an hour when every room is empty, and the scope says which rooms can be done while others sleep.

In a shared house booked for {subject} in {place}, an HMO pack at £561 where that published pack is the job means we ask the figure is not reused for a different combination of certificates, and the quote lists the items in the pack the client asked for.

In a shared house booked for {subject} in {place}, a selective licence coming up for renewal means we ask the agent wants the papers in date order, and we send what this visit produced and nothing that pretends to be a licence.

In a shared house booked for {subject} in {place}, a room used for storage that the licence still counts means we ask the visit includes it when the instruction says the licence requires it, and a locked store is not skipped in silence.
In a shared house booked for {subject} in {place}, external stairs to a flat over a shop means we ask the stair is part of the access and sometimes part of the job, and the quote says which.

In a shared house booked for {subject} in {place}, a house about to be let room by room for the first time means we ask the current layout is what we price, and a future partition is not included unless it is drawn and asked for.

In a shared house booked for {subject} in {place}, tenant changes every few months means we ask the report is written so the next manager can read it, and names of occupants are kept off the certificate unless the form requires them.

In a shared house booked for {subject} in {place}, a communal lounge that is also a corridor means we ask furniture in the escape is noted when the job is the escape, and we do not move people's belongings without being asked.

In a shared house booked for {subject} in {place}, meters in a cupboard on the stair means we ask the cupboard has to be opened for an electrical visit, and the key for it is requested with the other keys.

In a shared house booked for {subject} in {place}, a written house rule about visitors means we ask the engineer follows the access the manager has agreed, and we do not turn up on a different day to the one the residents were told.

In a shared house booked for {subject} in {place}, an additional kitchen in a rear extension means we ask the extension is named on the quote when the job includes it, and it is not assumed from a photograph of the front.

When an agent instructs {subject} in {place}, the invoice goes to the agency, not the tenant, so the report is copied to the address the agency named, and a tenant is not chased for a bill they were not asked to pay.
When an agent instructs {subject} in {place}, several branches share one landlord, so each branch wants its own paperwork, and the quote names the branch for that address.
When an agent instructs {subject} in {place}, the landlord is overseas, so the agent is the person who can accept the quote, and we do not wait on a time zone when the agent has authority.
When an agent instructs {subject} in {place}, a purchase order number is required, so the number is collected before the day, and the invoice can match the order the accounts team expect.

When an agent instructs {subject} in {place}, the agency uploads certificates to a portal, so we ask for the format they can actually upload, and a file they cannot open is sent again in the format they named.
When an agent instructs {subject} in {place}, one property manager covers the whole portfolio, so they cannot take a call for every arrival, and the day's list is emailed the afternoon before.
When an agent instructs {subject} in {place}, the instruction arrived from an assistant, so the approver is a different person, and the quote is addressed to the approver.
When an agent instructs {subject} in {place}, a maintenance float has a limit, so work above that limit needs a second approval, and the quote shows the line that would cross it.
When an agent instructs {subject} in {place}, the agency wants before-and-after photographs, so the photographs are of the work, not of the tenant's home life, and the email says what was taken.
When an agent instructs {subject} in {place}, two agents email about the same house, so we ask which instruction stands, and we do not start on contradictory scopes.
When an agent instructs {subject} in {place}, the landlord wants a copy as well as the agent, so both emails are on the quote, and the report is sent to each of them when that was asked for.
When an agent instructs {subject} in {place}, a new agent has just taken over the property, so the old certificates may still be in the previous portal, and we work from what this agent can send us.
When an agent instructs {subject} in {place}, the agency diary and our diary have to be compared, so a slot that suits only one of them is not confirmed, and the confirmed hour is written to both.

When an agent instructs {subject} in {place}, a statement of works is attached to the instruction, so the quote follows that statement or it marks the lines we cannot see, and silent omissions are not left for the invoice.
When an agent instructs {subject} in {place}, the agent will meet us at the first house only, so later houses need keys or tenants, and each address on the list has its own access note.
When an agent instructs {subject} in {place}, payment runs on a monthly certificate, so the job is still quoted before it is done, and the monthly run does not replace the written scope.

When an agent instructs {subject} in {place}, the landlord has asked the agent not to approve repairs over a stated amount, so that amount is respected, and a larger repair is returned as a separate quote.
When an agent instructs {subject} in {place}, the agency uses its own job reference, so our note quotes that reference, and the two systems can be matched later.
When an agent instructs {subject} in {place}, a clerk will raise the instruction only after the quote, so we do not attend on a verbal chase, and the written acceptance is what books the day.
When an agent instructs {subject} in {place}, the portfolio includes houses and flats, so each type is described as what it is, and a flat price is not pasted onto a house line.
When an agent instructs {subject} in {place}, the agent wants remedials listed separately from the test, so the quote does that, and a failed item is not quietly folded into the test fee.
When an agent instructs {subject} in {place}, a managing agent and a letting agent are both involved, so the quote says which of them instructed us, and reports go where that instruction asked.

Useful photographs before {subject} in {place} show the part that has failed and enough of the room to see the access, rather than a dark shot of a whole facade, so the engineer can tell what to bring.
Useful photographs before {subject} in {place} show the outside of the house, including the door we should use, rather than a picture that could be any terrace, so the right building is visited.

Useful photographs before {subject} in {place} show a written note of the symptom as well as the picture, rather than a photograph with no explanation, so the visit is aimed at the fault that was described.

Useful photographs before {subject} in {place} show the approach for materials, such as a narrow hall or a stair with a turn, rather than an assumption that everything will fit through the front door, so the quote allows for the carry when the photos show it.

Useful photographs before {subject} in {place} show the consumer unit, when the job is electrical, rather than a request for photographs of unrelated rooms, so the electrical visit starts from the board that was pictured.

Useful photographs before {subject} in {place} show the boiler and the programmer, when the job is heating, taken from a safe distance, rather than anyone removing a cover before the visit, so the engineer sees the appliance that is actually installed.

Useful photographs before {subject} in {place} show the vent, the actuator and the panel, when the job is smoke control, rather than a picture of the street only, so the AOV visit is prepared for the equipment on that stair.

Useful photographs before {subject} in {place} show the drive, the levels and the kerb, when the job is a driveway, rather than a single paving slab with no context, so the measure can be sketched before the survey.

Useful photographs before {subject} in {place} show the fence run, the posts and any gate, when the job is fencing, rather than a close-up that hides how long the boundary is, so the length is still checked on site.

Useful photographs before {subject} in {place} show the gully or the manhole, when the job is drainage, rather than a photograph of a wet floor with no outlet in frame, so the survey knows which cover to lift.

Useful photographs before {subject} in {place} show the slope and the stain, when the job is the roof, rather than a picture taken only from the pavement at night, so the leak that the household sees is the one we discuss.

Useful photographs before {subject} in {place} show the wall or the opening, when the job is demolition or a structural opening, rather than a request to knock through on the strength of a text message, so the design and the quote refer to the same opening.

Useful photographs before {subject} in {place} show the barrier arm and the cabinet, when the job is a barrier, rather than a photo of a bent boom with no label, so parts are identified from the cabinet that was pictured.

Useful photographs before {subject} in {place} show the appliance and the flue from a safe distance, when the job is gas, rather than a cover removed by the household, so the engineer attends the appliance that was named.

Useful photographs before {subject} in {place} show the rooms the certificate needs to cover, when the job is a landlord pack, rather than every cupboard in the house, so the pack is priced on the certificates that were asked for.
Useful photographs before {subject} in {place} show a date on the photograph, rather than an old listing picture presented as this week's fault, so the quote says if a fresh look is required.
Useful photographs before {subject} in {place} show the damage and a wider shot that shows where it sits, rather than a finger over the lens, so the scale of the repair can be discussed honestly.

Useful photographs before {subject} in {place} show access constraints such as a car that cannot be moved, rather than a clear drive in the photo and a blocked drive on the day, so the instruction is updated when the photo and the day will differ.

Useful photographs before {subject} in {place} show the existing equipment label when a part has to match, rather than a guess at the brand from the colour of the case, so the label is what the order is checked against.

Useful photographs before {subject} in {place} show only what the household is comfortable sharing, rather than photographs of people or personal papers, so the file contains the building, not the occupants' private life.

Useful photographs before {subject} in {place} show a short clip if a noise or an intermittent fault is the reason for the call, rather than a long video of every room, so the relevant seconds are the ones we ask for.
Useful photographs before {subject} in {place} show the photos that match this address, rather than a set taken at a different property in the portfolio, so each house keeps its own pictures.

Getting to {subject} in {place} has to allow for a rural lane where two vehicles cannot pass, so the household is asked about a passing place, and the arrival is timed when the lane is quiet if they have told us it matters.

Getting to {subject} in {place} has to allow for a hill with no handbrake-friendly stop, so the van is parked where it can be left safely, and the extra walk is included in the plan.
Getting to {subject} in {place} has to allow for event-day closures the household already knows about, so the visit is moved, and we do not keep a slot the streets cannot serve.
Getting to {subject} in {place} has to allow for a car park that belongs to a neighbouring business, so we do not use it without permission, and the instruction says where we have been told to park.

Getting to {subject} in {place} has to allow for a gated mews, so the code or the resident who can open it is on the booking, and the engineer is not stuck at the gate with the quote accepted and the day lost.
